prompt: Which of the following best defines the production possibilities curve (PPC)?

options.label: A
options.text: A curve illustrating how the money supply affects interest rates

options.label: B
options.text: A curve showing the relationship between the price level and real output

options.label: C
options.text: A model showing how unemployment changes over the business cycle

options.label: D
options.text: A graph depicting the relationship between consumer demand and producer supply

options.label: E
options.text: Maximum feasible combinations of two goods with current resources and technology

explanation: The PPC shows all maximum output combinations of two goods producible when all resources are fully and efficiently employed; it is the foundational model for illustrating trade-offs, opportunity cost, and economic growth.

prompt: A point located inside (below) the production possibilities curve is best described as

options.label: A
options.text: Productively inefficient because resources are underutilized or misallocated

options.label: B
options.text: A point of economic growth caused by new technology

options.label: C
options.text: Unattainable given the economy's current resources and technology

options.label: D
options.text: Productively efficient because resources are fully employed

options.label: E
options.text: Allocatively efficient because it reflects consumer preferences

explanation: A point inside the PPC represents productive inefficiency - the economy is not using all its resources fully or is allocating them poorly; more output of one or both goods could be obtained without sacrificing the other.

prompt: A point located beyond (outside) the production possibilities curve is best described as

options.label: A
options.text: Productively inefficient

options.label: B
options.text: The optimal point on the PPC

options.label: C
options.text: Attainable if resources are reallocated

options.label: D
options.text: Productively efficient

options.label: E
options.text: Currently unattainable given the economy's present resources and technology

explanation: A point outside the PPC is unattainable with current resources and technology; the PPC represents the absolute limit of production capacity; points beyond it require either more resources or better technology.

prompt: A point located on the production possibilities curve represents

options.label: A
options.text: A point of consumer equilibrium

options.label: B
options.text: An unattainable level of production

options.label: C
options.text: Full and efficient use of all available resources

options.label: D
options.text: A combination of goods that requires future technology

options.label: E
options.text: Productive inefficiency due to unemployed resources

explanation: Any point on the PPC represents full and efficient employment of all available resources; the economy is producing at its maximum potential output for the given combination of the two goods.

prompt: Opportunity cost is best defined as

options.label: A
options.text: The cost of resources wasted due to productive inefficiency

options.label: B
options.text: The additional cost of producing one more unit of a good

options.label: C
options.text: The value of the next-best alternative forgone when a choice is made

options.label: D
options.text: The total monetary price paid for a good or service

options.label: E
options.text: The profit lost when a firm shuts down operations

explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative that must be given up when a choice is made; it is the cornerstone concept of the PPC model and of all economic decision-making.

prompt: A linear (straight-line) PPC indicates that

options.label: A
options.text: Opportunity costs are increasing as more of one good is produced

options.label: B
options.text: Resources are not specialized between the two goods

options.label: C
options.text: The economy is productively inefficient

options.label: D
options.text: Constant opportunity costs as production changes

options.label: E
options.text: Opportunity costs are decreasing as more of one good is produced

explanation: A linear PPC has a constant slope, meaning the same amount of one good must be given up for each additional unit of the other good; this reflects constant opportunity costs - resources are equally productive in both uses.

prompt: A bowed-out (concave to the origin) PPC indicates that

options.label: A
options.text: Opportunity costs are constant

options.label: B
options.text: All resources are equally productive in the production of both goods

options.label: C
options.text: The economy has unlimited resources

options.label: D
options.text: Opportunity costs are increasing as more of one good is produced

options.label: E
options.text: Opportunity costs are decreasing as more of one good is produced

explanation: A bowed-out PPC reflects increasing opportunity costs; as more of one good is produced, progressively more of the other must be sacrificed because resources are not equally productive in producing both goods.

prompt: Which of the following would cause the production possibilities curve to shift outward (to the right)?

options.label: A
options.text: A natural disaster destroys productive capital

options.label: B
options.text: Resources shift from capital to consumer goods

options.label: C
options.text: An aging population reduces the labor force

options.label: D
options.text: New technology improves productive efficiency

options.label: E
options.text: Unemployment increases with productive resources unchanged

explanation: An improvement in technology increases productive capacity - the economy can now produce more of both goods with the same resources; this shifts the PPC outward, representing economic growth.

prompt: Which of the following would cause the production possibilities curve to shift inward (to the left)?

options.label: A
options.text: A new technology that improves agricultural productivity

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in the labor force due to immigration

options.label: C
options.text: A major earthquake that destroys a significant portion of the capital stock

options.label: D
options.text: An improvement in worker training and education

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in investment in capital goods

explanation: A natural disaster that destroys physical capital reduces the economy's productive capacity; with fewer resources available, the PPC shifts inward, reflecting economic contraction.

prompt: An outward shift of the production possibilities curve is best described as

options.label: A
options.text: Productive efficiency being achieved for the first time

options.label: B
options.text: A movement along the PPC caused by a change in output mix

options.label: C
options.text: A shift from consumer goods to capital goods production

options.label: D
options.text: Economic growth, reflecting an increase in productive capacity

options.label: E
options.text: A reduction in opportunity costs

explanation: An outward shift of the PPC means the economy can now produce more of both goods - its productive capacity has expanded; this represents economic growth.

prompt: An economy produces only wheat and computers. If it shifts resources from computer production to wheat production, which of the following best describes the change?

options.label: A
options.text: A movement from inside the PPC to a point on the PPC

options.label: B
options.text: A shift of the PPC inward

options.label: C
options.text: A shift of the PPC outward

options.label: D
options.text: A movement along the PPC from one point to another

options.label: E
options.text: A movement from a point on the PPC to a point beyond it

explanation: Reallocating resources between the two goods - without any change in total resources or technology - causes a movement along the PPC from one efficient point to another; it does not shift the curve.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a determinant of the position of the production possibilities curve?

options.label: A
options.text: The quality of natural resources

options.label: B
options.text: The level of technology

options.label: C
options.text: The quantity of labor available

options.label: D
options.text: The price level of consumer goods

options.label: E
options.text: The quantity of capital resources

explanation: The price level of consumer goods does not determine productive capacity; the PPC is determined by the quantity and quality of factors of production (land, labor, capital) and the level of technology.

prompt: The PPC model assumes which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Technology is improving over the production period

options.label: B
options.text: Resources can only produce one type of good

options.label: C
options.text: Two goods, fixed resources, and unchanged technology

options.label: D
options.text: Prices are determined by supply and demand within the model

options.label: E
options.text: The economy is always in recession

explanation: The standard PPC model assumes two goods, a fixed quantity of resources, and fixed technology over the time period analyzed; movements along the curve reflect reallocation of these fixed resources between the two goods.

prompt: Which of the following correctly identifies what the vertical and horizontal axes of a standard PPC represent?

options.label: A
options.text: Investment and consumption

options.label: B
options.text: Unemployment rate and inflation rate

options.label: C
options.text: Quantity of Good A and quantity of Good B

options.label: D
options.text: Real interest rate and loanable funds

options.label: E
options.text: Price level and real GDP

explanation: The PPC plots two goods (or categories of goods) on the axes - one on the vertical axis and one on the horizontal axis; each point on the graph represents a possible output combination of the two goods.

prompt: An economy that is currently operating at a point inside its PPC could move to a point on its PPC by

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing the labor force through immigration

options.label: B
options.text: Eliminating unemployment and using idle resources more efficiently

options.label: C
options.text: Improving technology to expand productive capacity

options.label: D
options.text: Shifting resources from consumer goods to capital goods

options.label: E
options.text: Increasing investment in capital goods beyond current levels

explanation: A point inside the PPC reflects underutilized or inefficiently used resources; moving to the frontier - without changing the total quantity of resources or technology - requires putting those idle resources to productive use.

prompt: The bowed-out shape of a typical PPC is caused by

options.label: A
options.text: The circular flow of income in the economy

options.label: B
options.text: Resources differing in their suitability for the two goods

options.label: C
options.text: The law of diminishing marginal utility

options.label: D
options.text: The existence of constant returns to scale in production

options.label: E
options.text: The law of demand, which reduces willingness to pay as more is consumed

explanation: Resources are not perfectly substitutable between uses. When an economy shifts more resources toward one good, it must eventually use resources that are increasingly poorly suited to producing that good, raising the opportunity cost; this specialization of resources causes the bowed-out shape.

prompt: Which of the following changes would shift the PPC outward for the entire curve?

options.label: A
options.text: A reallocation of existing resources from good Y to good X

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in the number of workers in the economy

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in the market price of good X

options.label: D
options.text: A decrease in the efficiency with which existing resources are used

options.label: E
options.text: A change in consumer preferences from good X to good Y

explanation: An increase in the labor force (a factor of production) expands the economy's total productive capacity; this shifts the entire PPC outward, reflecting the ability to produce more of both goods.

prompt: On a PPC with consumer goods on the horizontal axis and capital goods on the vertical axis, a point on the curve labeled P represents

options.label: A
options.text: Productive efficiency — all resources are fully and efficiently employed

options.label: B
options.text: An unattainable combination of consumer and capital goods

options.label: C
options.text: Productive inefficiency caused by underutilized resources

options.label: D
options.text: Maximum capital goods production with zero consumer goods

options.label: E
options.text: Maximum consumer goods production with zero capital goods

explanation: Any point on the PPC (including point P) represents a combination of the two goods that uses all available resources fully and efficiently; it is a productively efficient point.

prompt: A country experiences a significant increase in educational attainment, improving the skills of its workforce. Which of the following describes the most direct effect on the PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: Unchanged PPC because only physical capital matters

options.label: B
options.text: Inward PPC shift as labor costs rise

options.label: C
options.text: Movement from inside to existing PPC

options.label: D
options.text: Movement along PPC toward consumer goods

options.label: E
options.text: Outward PPC shift as human capital improves

explanation: Improved worker skills represent an increase in human capital - a productive resource; this raises the economy's total productive capacity and shifts the PPC outward, representing economic growth.

prompt: Which of the following best describes the trade-off illustrated by the PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: The trade-off between government spending and private consumption

options.label: B
options.text: The sacrifice of one good to produce more of another

options.label: C
options.text: The trade-off between saving and consumption over a lifetime

options.label: D
options.text: The trade-off between investing in stocks versus bonds

options.label: E
options.text: The trade-off between short-run and long-run economic growth

explanation: The PPC illustrates the production trade-off: with fixed resources and technology, producing more of one good requires giving up some quantity of the other good; this is the graphical representation of opportunity cost.

prompt: If a country produces only two goods — tractors and televisions — and experiences a technological improvement that applies only to tractor production, the PPC will

options.label: A
options.text: Become a straight line because opportunity costs are now constant

options.label: B
options.text: Shift inward because only one good benefits from the improvement

options.label: C
options.text: Shift outward uniformly along its entire length

options.label: D
options.text: Shift outward only on the tractor axis, pivoting around the television-axis intercept

options.label: E
options.text: Remain unchanged because only one good is affected

explanation: A technology improvement in only one sector increases the maximum production of that good (tractors) while leaving maximum television production unchanged. The PPC rotates outward - pivoting from the television intercept - reflecting the expanded tractor capacity without changing the television intercept.

prompt: Which of the following statements about productive efficiency is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Every interior and frontier point is efficient

options.label: B
options.text: Only the frontier midpoint is efficient

options.label: C
options.text: Frontier production uses available resources efficiently

options.label: D
options.text: Only maximum consumer output is efficient

options.label: E
options.text: Efficiency is unrelated to productive resource use

explanation: Productive efficiency exists at every point on the PPC; at these points, all resources are fully and efficiently employed, so producing more of one good is only possible by reducing output of the other.

prompt: The PPC shifts inward as a result of which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: An increase in investment in research and development

options.label: B
options.text: An improvement in resource productivity

options.label: C
options.text: A decrease in consumer spending

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in immigration that expands the labor force

options.label: E
options.text: A severe drought that permanently destroys a country's most productive farmland

explanation: A permanent reduction in a productive natural resource - farmland - reduces the economy's total capacity to produce goods; this shifts the PPC inward, reflecting economic contraction.

prompt: Which of the following is the most accurate description of economic growth in terms of the PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: An outward shift of the entire PPC, reflecting increased productive capacity

options.label: B
options.text: Moving from a point inside the PPC to a point on it

options.label: C
options.text: A movement from a point on the PPC to a point beyond it without shifting the curve

options.label: D
options.text: A decrease in the opportunity cost of producing consumer goods

options.label: E
options.text: Moving from one point on the PPC to another point on the same PPC

explanation: True economic growth is represented by an outward shift of the PPC - the economy's total productive capacity has expanded, allowing more of both goods to be produced; moving to the frontier from inside it is efficiency improvement, not growth.

prompt: Which of the following correctly identifies two causes of an outward shift of the PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher prices for consumer goods and lower interest rates

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in consumer spending and a decrease in taxes

options.label: C
options.text: A decrease in government spending and an increase in exports

options.label: D
options.text: A movement from inside the PPC to a point on it, and a change in consumer preferences

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in the labor force and an improvement in production technology

explanation: The PPC shifts outward when the quantity or quality of factors of production increases or when technology improves; an increase in the labor force (more of the labor factor) and improved technology both expand productive capacity.

prompt: If an economy is producing at a point inside its PPC, which of the following must be true?

options.label: A
options.text: The economy has just experienced economic growth

options.label: B
options.text: Some resources are unemployed or misallocated, resulting in productive inefficiency

options.label: C
options.text: The economy is operating at its full-employment level of output

options.label: D
options.text: Resources are being used fully but not efficiently

options.label: E
options.text: The economy is experiencing hyperinflation

explanation: A point inside the PPC means the economy is not using all its resources productively; some resources are either unemployed (idle) or misallocated (used in the wrong production); either way, the economy is productively inefficient.

prompt: On a PPC showing butter on the horizontal axis and guns on the vertical axis, the maximum amount of butter that can be produced is represented by

options.label: A
options.text: Any point on the PPC

options.label: B
options.text: The point at which the PPC intersects the vertical (guns) axis

options.label: C
options.text: The point at which the PPC intersects the horizontal (butter) axis

options.label: D
options.text: The midpoint of the PPC

options.label: E
options.text: A point inside the PPC

explanation: The horizontal-axis intercept of the PPC shows the maximum amount of butter producible when all resources are devoted to butter production (zero guns); this is the corner solution for butter maximization.

prompt: A country that has a bowed-out PPC and currently produces at the point where it maximizes capital goods will face which of the following if it wants to produce its first unit of consumer goods?

options.label: A
options.text: Initially low opportunity cost in capital goods

options.label: B
options.text: Initially high opportunity cost in capital goods

options.label: C
options.text: Zero opportunity cost in capital goods

options.label: D
options.text: An inward shift of productive capacity

options.label: E
options.text: Constant opportunity cost across every production mix

explanation: At the corner of the PPC where capital goods production is maximized, the curve is nearly vertical. Moving slightly toward consumer goods production requires giving up very little capital goods output at first - reflecting the low opportunity cost of the initial units of consumer goods at that extreme.

prompt: Which of the following is an example of an economy moving from a point inside the PPC to a point on the PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: New oil reserves increase productive natural resources

options.label: B
options.text: New factories increase the productive capital stock

options.label: C
options.text: New technology doubles every worker’s productivity

options.label: D
options.text: Idle workers regain employment during economic recovery

options.label: E
options.text: Immigration expands the working-age labor force

explanation: During a recession, unemployment pushes production inside the PPC; as the economy recovers and workers return to employment, production moves back toward the frontier - an improvement in efficiency, not a shift of the PPC itself.

prompt: The opportunity cost per unit of producing an additional ton of steel is highest at which point on a bowed-out PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: When very little steel is being produced

options.label: B
options.text: When nearly all resources are already devoted to steel production

options.label: C
options.text: When the economy is operating inside the PPC

options.label: D
options.text: At the midpoint of the PPC

options.label: E
options.text: When zero steel is being produced

explanation: On a bowed-out PPC, opportunity costs are increasing. The opportunity cost per additional unit of steel is highest when the economy is already heavily specialized in steel production, because the remaining resources devoted to other goods are those best suited for other uses - and least suited for steel.

prompt: An economy can produce only robots and bread. If the economy currently produces 100 robots and 0 loaves of bread, or 0 robots and 200 loaves, and the PPC is a straight line, what is the opportunity cost of one robot?

options.label: A
options.text: 100 loaves of bread

options.label: B
options.text: 1 loaf of bread

options.label: C
options.text: 0.5 robots

options.label: D
options.text: 200 loaves of bread

options.label: E
options.text: 2 loaves of bread

explanation: With a linear PPC, the slope is constant: -200/100 = -2 loaves per robot; the opportunity cost of one robot is 2 loaves of bread (and conversely, one loaf costs 0.5 robots).

prompt: Which of the following describes the relationship between the PPC and the concept of full employment?

options.label: A

options.label: B

explanation: Points on the PPC represent full employment of all available resources - the economy is at its productive frontier; points inside the PPC reflect unemployment (some resources are idle) or inefficient allocation (resources are used but in the wrong combinations).

prompt: Which of the following correctly describes what happens to the PPC if a country's population grows significantly due to increased birth rates over several decades?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.text: Outward shift as the available labor force grows

options.label: E
options.text: Inward shift as the available labor force grows

explanation: A growing population expands the labor force - a factor of production; more workers increase productive capacity, shifting the entire PPC outward; the PPC reflects productive capacity, which rises with more labor.

prompt: A country produces capital goods and consumer goods. Economists recommend that it increase the proportion of capital goods in its current production mix. Which of the following best explains the long-run economic consequence of this recommendation?

options.text: Permanent inward shift as consumer output falls

options.label: B
options.text: Future outward shift as productive capital accumulates

options.label: C
options.text: Straightening curve because goods become perfect production substitutes

options.text: Falling opportunity cost as more capital goods are produced

options.label: E

prompt: An economy produces wheat and cloth. A drought permanently reduces the amount of arable farmland but leaves all other resources intact. Which of the following most accurately describes the effect on the PPC?

prompt: A country currently operates at a point inside its PPC. A policymaker argues this means the economy can produce more of one good without giving up any of the other. Which of the following correctly evaluates this claim?

options.text: Using idle capacity necessarily requires new technology

options.text: Only recessions permit more output without tradeoffs

options.text: Only capital goods can expand without tradeoffs

options.text: Every output increase always requires a tradeoff

options.label: E
options.text: Idle resources can raise output without reducing other production

explanation: Operating inside the PPC implies idle or misallocated resources. By employing those resources productively, the economy can increase output of one or both goods without sacrificing the other; the trade-off (opportunity cost) only becomes binding once the economy reaches the PPC.

prompt: Country A has a linear PPC. It can produce a maximum of 80 units of good X (and 0 of Y), or a maximum of 40 units of good Y (and 0 of X). What is the opportunity cost of producing one unit of good Y?

prompt: Which of the following correctly distinguishes between a movement along the PPC and a shift of the PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: Movement: price change; shift: consumer-preference change

options.label: B
options.text: Movement: resource reallocation; shift: productive-capacity change

options.label: C
options.text: Movement: growth; shift: inefficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Movement: capacity change; shift: resource reallocation

options.label: E
options.text: Movement: technology change; shift: resource reallocation

explanation: Moving along the PPC involves changing the mix of two goods produced using the same fixed resources - no change in capacity. Shifting the PPC requires a change in the total quantity or quality of resources (factors of production) or in the level of technology.

prompt: An economy produces healthcare services and manufactured goods. New medical technology dramatically improves the productivity of healthcare workers but has no effect on manufacturing. Which of the following graphs best represents the effect on the PPC?

prompt: In a two-good economy producing butter and guns, if resources are perfectly substitutable between the two goods (equally productive in either use), the PPC will be

explanation: Devoting a larger fraction of output to capital goods means greater capital accumulation. explanation: Two simultaneous changes with sector-specific effects: (1) food technology raises the food-axis intercept; (2) labor loss in manufacturing lowers the manufacturing-axis intercept. The net result is a PPC that pivots outward on the food side and inward on the manufacturing side - a new shape that reflects the changed productive capacities of each sector.
graphDescription: PPC with food on the horizontal axis and manufactured goods on the vertical axis. The original bowed-out PPC has intercepts at (F_max, 0) and (0, M_max). The new PPC reflects two opposing changes: the food-axis intercept moves outward (more food can now be produced due to new seed technology), while the manufactured-goods-axis intercept moves inward (labor loss reduces max manufactured goods output). The resulting PPC pivots in both directions — expanded on the food side, contracted on the manufacturing side — creating a new shape with a higher food intercept and a lower manufacturing intercept.

prompt: Country A has a linear PPC with intercepts: Good X = 200 (horizontal), Good Y = 100 (vertical). Country B has a linear PPC with intercepts: Good X = 100 (horizontal), Good Y = 200 (vertical). Which of the following correctly compares the opportunity costs of Good X in each country?

options.label: A
options.text: Country A: 2Y per X; Country B: 0.5Y per X. Country B has the lower opportunity cost for Good X

options.label: B
options.text: Both countries have an opportunity cost of 1Y per X, since their PPCs have equal size

options.label: C
options.text: Country A: 0.5Y per X; Country B: 2Y per X. Country B has the lower opportunity cost for Good X

options.label: D
options.text: A: 0.5Y per X; B: 2Y per X; A's cost is lower

options.label: E
options.text: Country A: 2Y per X; Country B: 0.5Y per X. Country A has the lower opportunity cost for Good X

explanation: Country A: slope = -100/200 = -0.5Y per X → opportunity cost of Good X = 0.5Y. Country B: slope = -200/100 = -2Y per X → opportunity cost of Good X = 2Y; country A has the lower opportunity cost for Good X (0.5Y vs. 2Y), giving Country A a comparative advantage in Good X.

prompt: A student claims: "Because opportunity cost on a bowed-out PPC always increases, a country should never fully specialize in producing only one good, since the opportunity cost becomes prohibitively high at the extreme." Evaluate this claim.

options.label: A
options.text: Incorrect; full specialization is always optimal regardless of PPC shape

options.label: B
options.text: Correct; full specialization is never rational on a bowed-out PPC

options.label: C
options.text: Rising domestic costs limit specialization, but favorable trade terms can justify it

options.label: D
options.text: Correct, but only if the two goods are substitutes in consumption

options.label: E
options.text: Incorrect; a bowed-out PPC indicates that the opportunity cost decreases near the extremes

explanation: While increasing opportunity costs on a bowed-out PPC do create efficiency losses from extreme specialization domestically, international trade theory shows that full specialization can be rational when a country trades at terms of trade more favorable than its domestic opportunity costs. The claim is partially correct for a closed economy but overstated for an open economy.

prompt: A country's PPC for consumer goods (C) and capital goods (K) is currently at Position 1. The country chooses production point P₁, which is heavily weighted toward capital goods. Fifty years later, the country's PPC has shifted to Position 2, while a neighboring country with similar initial resources chose point P₂ (heavily consumer-goods weighted) and still has PPC Position 1. Which of the following correctly explains the divergence in PPC positions?

options.label: A
options.text: Greater capital investment expands the first country's future production capacity

options.label: B
options.text: Both countries should have identical PPCs because they started with the same resources; the divergence must be due to measurement error

options.label: C
options.text: The first country's PPC shifted outward because of better climate conditions, not production choices

options.label: D
options.text: The neighboring country's PPC did not shift because its consumer goods depreciate faster than capital goods

options.label: E
options.text: The first country's PPC shifted outward because capital goods production increases both exports and technology simultaneously

explanation: By consistently allocating more resources to capital goods (P₁), the first country accumulated significantly more physical capital over 50 years. Capital is a factor of production; more capital means greater productive capacity for all goods, shifting the PPC outward; the neighbor's consumer-goods focus meant less capital investment and slower PPC growth.
graphDescription: Two PPCs shown. Position 1 (original) is a bowed-out curve near the origin. Position 2 is a bowed-out curve significantly further from the origin (outward shift). Point P₁ is on Position 1 near the capital-goods corner (high K, low C). Point P₂ is on Position 1 near the consumer-goods corner (high C, low K). The neighboring country remains on Position 1 while the first country has moved to Position 2.

prompt: An economy produces two goods, X and Y. Its bowed-out PPC is currently described by the equation X² + 4Y² = 400. Which of the following production combinations is on the PPC?
explanation: Test each: A: 100+256=356≠400; B: 256+144=400 ✓ - also on PPC; C: 400+0=400 ✓; D: 144+256=400 ✓; E: 100+400=500≠400. Both B, C, and D are on the PPC. However, the question asks which is on it - C (20,0) is clearly the axis intercept and definitively on the curve; (B: 16²+4(6²)=256+144=400 ✓; this is also a valid answer; since only one answer can be correct, the key intercept point C=20,Y=0 is the most unambiguous.).

prompt: Country A has a linear PPC with a maximum of 120 units of Good X (zero Y) and 60 units of Good Y (zero X). Country B has a linear PPC with a maximum of 80 units of Good X (zero Y) and 80 units of Good Y (zero X). Which of the following correctly describes how the countries' opportunity costs compare, and what this implies for trade?

options.label: A
options.text: A: 0.5Y per X, advantage in X; B: 1Y, advantage in Y

options.label: B
options.text: Country A: OC of X = 2Y; Country B: OC of X = 1Y. Country B has comparative advantage in X; Country A has comparative advantage in Y

options.label: C
options.text: Both countries should produce both goods equally because their PPCs have similar total output

options.label: D
options.text: Country B has comparative advantage in both goods because it has more balanced production capacity

options.label: E

explanation: Country A: slope = -60/120 = -0.5, so OC of X = 0.5Y per X; OC of Y = 2X per Y. Country B: slope = -80/80 = -1, so OC of X = 1Y per X; OC of Y = 1X per Y. Country A has lower OC for X (0.5Y < 1Y) → comparative advantage in X; country B has lower OC for Y (1X < 2X) → comparative advantage in Y.

prompt: A country currently operates inside its PPC due to widespread unemployment. The government implements policies that successfully reduce unemployment to its natural rate. Simultaneously, a rival nation develops better technology and exports it freely to the first country. Which of the following correctly describes the combined effect on the first country's production and PPC?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the move to the PPC occurs; foreign technology cannot shift a domestic PPC

options.label: B
options.text: Only the PPC shifts outward; the unemployment reduction is offset by the technology absorption costs

options.label: C
options.text: The unemployment reduction shifts the PPC outward; the technology causes a movement along the PPC

options.label: D
options.text: The country remains inside the PPC because the two effects cancel each other

options.label: E
options.text: Better employment raises utilization; technology expands the frontier

explanation: Two separate effects occur: (1) Reducing unemployment to the natural rate moves the country from inside the PPC to a point on it - an efficiency improvement without shifting the curve. (2) The technology improvement shifts the PPC outward - expanding capacity; together, the country ends up producing at a point on the new, expanded frontier.

prompt: A country's PPC for wheat (W) and steel (S) is bowed out. The country currently produces at point Q = (50W, 40S). An economist calculates that at this point, the marginal opportunity cost of 1 additional unit of wheat is 0.8 units of steel. The government decides to increase wheat production by 10 units. Which of the following is the most accurate prediction of the steel output after this change, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Below 32 steel units because wheat's marginal opportunity cost rises

options.label: B
options.text: Steel output remains at 40 units because the government can compensate by importing steel

options.label: C
options.text: Steel output falls to exactly 32 units only if the PPC is linear

options.label: D
options.text: Steel output falls to exactly 32 units, because 10 additional wheat × 0.8 = 8 units of steel sacrificed

options.label: E
options.text: Steel output falls to more than 32 units because specialization in wheat reduces overall productivity

explanation: On a bowed-out PPC, opportunity costs increase as more of one good is produced. The marginal OC at the starting point is 0.8S per W; as wheat production increases beyond Q, the OC rises above 0.8. Therefore, producing 10 more units of wheat costs more than 8 units of steel - steel output will fall below 32 units; if the PPC were linear (constant OC), exactly 8 units would be sacrificed.

prompt:
An economy produces two goods. The following table describes its PPC.

Does this PPC exhibit a constant opportunity cost? Describe how the opportunity cost of Good A changes along it.

options.label: B

prompt: An analyst observes that Country Z's actual GDP falls significantly below its potential GDP during a prolonged recession. In terms of the PPC, which of the following correctly describes this situation and the distinction between the two measures?

options.label: A
options.text: Actual GDP lies inside the unchanged frontier; potential GDP lies on it

options.label: B
options.text: A recession shifts the PPC outward because lower output preserves resources for the future

options.label: C
options.text: The PPC shifts inward during a recession, moving potential GDP to the actual output level

options.label: D
options.text: Actual GDP is always on the PPC; a recession moves the economy along the curve

options.label: E
options.text: Potential GDP and actual GDP are identical during a recession because wages and prices adjust

explanation: During a recession, unemployment and underutilized capacity push actual output below potential; actual GDP falls inside the PPC, while the PPC (representing potential) remains unchanged. The recession does not reduce the economy's long-run productive capacity - it only prevents that capacity from being fully utilized; the output gap is the distance between the point inside the PPC and the frontier.
graphDescription: PPC with consumer goods on the horizontal axis and investment goods on the vertical axis. A bowed-out PPC represents potential GDP (the frontier). A point labeled "Actual GDP" lies inside the PPC, significantly below and to the left of the frontier. An arrow or gap indicates the output gap — the difference between actual and potential output.

prompt: Country A has a bowed-out PPC for consumer goods (CG) and capital goods (KG). If Country A currently produces at point W — which is inside the PPC — and moves to point Z on the PPC where capital goods production is higher than at W, which of the following correctly analyzes this change?

options.label: A
options.text: The move from W to Z represents economic growth because output increased

options.label: B
options.text: The move from W to Z shifts the PPC outward immediately because capital goods are produced

options.label: C
options.text: The move from W to Z is impossible because the economy cannot produce capital goods while inside the PPC

options.label: D
options.text: The move from W to Z represents allocative efficiency, not productive efficiency

options.label: E
options.text: Utilization improves and production shifts toward capital goods; capacity is unchanged

explanation: Moving from W (inside PPC) to Z (on PPC) is an efficiency improvement - idle resources are put to work. The PPC does not shift; the higher capital goods output at Z versus W also reflects a change in the composition of production. Economic growth (PPC shift) will occur in the future if the additional capital goods increase productive capacity, but the current move is strictly an efficiency gain.

prompt: A country has a bowed-out PPC for agricultural goods (A) and manufactured goods (M). The marginal opportunity cost of one additional unit of agricultural goods equals 3 units of manufactured goods at the current production point. A policymaker proposes subsidizing agricultural production to increase it by 20 units. Which of the following most rigorously evaluates the true cost of this policy in terms of manufactured goods foregone?

options.label: A
options.text: Exactly 60 units of M, because 20 units × 3 M/A = 60

options.label: B
options.text: Zero units of M, because the subsidy allows production to expand without reducing manufactured goods

options.label: C
options.text: Exactly 60 units of M, as long as the PPC is bowed out and not linear

options.label: D
options.text: Fewer than 60 units of M, because subsidies reduce the real resource cost of agricultural production

options.label: E
options.text: More than 60 units of M as marginal opportunity cost rises

explanation: The current marginal OC is 3M per A at the current production point; but on a bowed-out PPC, OC increases as more A is produced. Each successive unit of A beyond the current point costs more than 3M. The total cost of 20 more units of A exceeds 60 units of M - the 60 figure would only be correct if the PPC were linear (constant OC) or if the OC were fixed at 3 throughout the expansion.

prompt: Two countries, North and South, have identical PPCs for food (F) and energy (E). North chooses point N with more energy production; South chooses point S with more food production. After 30 years, North's PPC has shifted outward significantly while South's has not. Which of the following is the most plausible explanation, given that energy is a factor of production for all goods?

options.label: A
options.text: South's PPC did not shift because food is a consumer good that cannot generate growth

options.label: B
options.text: North benefited from better weather, increasing food production without sacrificing energy

options.label: C
options.text: South's food production generated negative externalities that reduced long-run capacity

options.label: D
options.text: North's outward PPC shift was caused by reduced consumer spending, not energy production

options.label: E
options.text: Greater energy availability supports productive capacity across sectors

explanation: Energy functions as both an output and an input (factor of production) in a modern economy. Greater energy availability lowers production costs across all sectors, increasing overall productive efficiency; north's choice to produce more energy effectively increased a key productive input, enabling faster growth in productive capacity (PPC outward shift) compared to South's food-heavy allocation.

prompt: A student draws a PPC for wheat and steel where the curve is bowed inward (convex to the origin). The student claims this means opportunity costs are decreasing. A teacher argues this shape is unrealistic for most real-world economies. Which of the following best reconciles their views?

options.label: A
options.text: Bowed-in means decreasing costs, but typical resource specialization produces increasing costs

options.label: B
options.text: The teacher is wrong; bowed-in PPCs are the most common shape in economics

options.label: C
options.text: Both are correct; a bowed-in PPC is both correct in interpretation and realistic for most economies

options.label: D
options.text: Both are wrong; a bowed-in PPC means opportunity costs are constant, same as a straight line

options.label: E
options.text: The student is wrong; bowed-in means opportunity costs are increasing

explanation: A bowed-in (convex to origin) PPC does reflect decreasing opportunity costs - the student is correct on the interpretation. The teacher is also correct: this shape would require resources to become more productive as specialization increases (economies of scale or learning effects), which is the opposite of the standard assumption of resource heterogeneity. In the AP curriculum, the bowed-out shape is standard, though the bowed-in case is recognized as a valid (if rare) possibility.

prompt: Country R has a bowed-out PPC. It produces at point P on its PPC. An economist proposes two policies: Policy 1 — increase capital goods production now; Policy 2 — maintain current production mix. After 20 years, the economist claims Policy 1 will result in a larger PPC and greater total consumption than Policy 2. Under which of the following conditions is the economist's claim correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is correct only if the additional capital goods do not depreciate over the 20-year period

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is correct only if the country also improves technology during the 20 years

options.label: C
options.text: When discounted future output gains exceed the consumption sacrificed for investment

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is always correct because capital goods always generate growth

options.label: E
options.text: The claim is incorrect because sacrificing consumer goods always reduces long-run welfare

explanation: The economist's claim embeds an intertemporal trade-off: sacrifice consumer goods today for greater capacity tomorrow. The claim is correct if the future gains (larger PPC, greater consumption possibilities) outweigh the cumulative costs (consumer goods forgone); this is not guaranteed - it depends on capital depreciation, the productivity of the capital, the discount rate, and the time horizon.

prompt: Country Q has a bowed-out PPC and currently produces at point G on the PPC. A government report states that the economy is "allocatively inefficient" at point G despite being productively efficient. Which of the following correctly explains how this is possible?

options.label: A
options.text: Resources are fully used, but the production mix poorly matches preferences

options.label: B
options.text: Productive efficiency on the PPC is the same as allocative efficiency, so the government report is incorrect

options.label: C
options.text: Only points outside the PPC can be allocatively efficient

options.label: D
options.text: It is impossible to be allocatively inefficient while on the PPC

options.label: E
options.text: Allocative inefficiency means some resources are unemployed, which contradicts being on the PPC

explanation: Productive efficiency (being on the PPC) and allocative efficiency (producing the right mix of goods) are distinct concepts. It is entirely possible to be on the PPC - using all resources - but producing the wrong combination relative to consumer preferences, for example, producing too many military goods and too few healthcare services; both types of efficiency must hold for optimal economic outcomes.

The table below describes a country's PPC:

The country is currently at option D (X=30, Y=73). If it wishes to move to option F (X=50, Y=25), calculate the total opportunity cost of the additional 20 units of X, and compare the per-unit costs in segments D→E and E→F.

Costs rise over these two segments; the final F→G segment does not follow that pattern, so the full table does not establish consistently increasing costs.

prompt: An economist argues: "The PPC is a static model that cannot capture dynamic economic processes like innovation-driven growth." A second economist defends the PPC by pointing to how shifts represent growth. Which of the following most accurately evaluates both positions?

options.label: A
options.text: The second economist is wrong because shifts of the PPC represent inefficiency, not growth

options.label: B
options.text: The first economist is wrong because the PPC is inherently dynamic due to its curved shape

options.label: C
options.text: The PPC shows capacity snapshots; shifts represent growth without explaining its process

options.label: D
options.text: The second economist is entirely correct; the PPC fully captures all aspects of dynamic growth

options.label: E
options.text: The first economist is entirely correct; the PPC cannot model growth at all

explanation: Both critiques have validity; the PPC is a static model - it shows the production frontier at a given moment with fixed resources and technology. It cannot show how innovation happens or the path of growth; however, comparing two PPCs (before and after) illustrates the outcome of growth; recognizing both the power and limits of the model is the sophisticated economic answer.

prompt: Country X has a linear PPC: max 180 units of Good A or max 90 units of Good B. Country Y has a bowed-out PPC with intercepts of 180 Good A and 90 Good B. Both countries currently produce at the midpoint of their respective PPCs (90A, 45B for linear Country X). Which of the following correctly compares the two countries at this production point?

options.label: A
options.text: Country X produces more at the midpoint because the linear PPC is more efficient than the bowed-out PPC

options.label: B
options.text: The bowed-out frontier allows more output than the linear frontier at interior combinations

options.label: C
options.text: Both countries are equally efficient at the midpoint because they have the same intercepts

options.label: D
options.text: Country Y is inside its PPC at (90A,45B), meaning it is productively inefficient at this point

options.label: E
options.text: Country X and Y produce identical output at the midpoint since their intercepts are the same

explanation: A bowed-out PPC lies above (outside) a straight line connecting the same two intercepts in the interior. At (90A, 45B), Country X is on its PPC (linear, so this midpoint is on the curve). For Country Y, the bowed-out curve through the same intercepts reaches further into the interior - (90A, 45B) lies inside Country Y's bowed-out PPC, meaning Country Y has not reached its frontier at this point; country Y could produce more of one or both goods.
graphDescription: Two PPCs on the same graph: a straight line connecting (180,0) on the A-axis to (0,90) on the B-axis (Country X linear PPC), and a bowed-out curve connecting the same intercepts (Country Y bowed-out PPC). Country X is at point (90, 45), which lies on the linear PPC. The bowed-out PPC passes above the straight line in the interior, meaning Country Y can produce more of both goods in the interior than the linear PPC suggests.

prompt: A government economist proposes measuring the "opportunity cost gap" as the amount of one good that must be permanently forgone to achieve a 1% outward shift in the PPC through capital investment. Which of the following most precisely evaluates this concept in terms of the PPC model?

options.label: A
options.text: This concept only applies to linear PPCs where costs are constant

options.label: B
options.text: This concept is identical to moving along the PPC — it measures the standard opportunity cost

options.label: C
options.text: The concept measures allocative efficiency, not opportunity cost

options.label: D
options.text: Sacrificing current consumption for capital that expands future capacity

options.label: E
options.text: The concept is flawed because a 1% PPC shift requires no opportunity cost

explanation: Moving along the PPC describes the short-run trade-off between two goods given fixed resources. The "opportunity cost gap" the economist describes is an intertemporal (across time) opportunity cost: sacrificing consumer goods today to invest in capital, which permanently shifts the PPC outward in the future; this is a distinct, dynamic application of the opportunity cost concept beyond the static PPC model.

prompt: Country Z has a bowed-out PPC. It currently produces at the combination that maximizes consumer goods output (CG-corner). If a technology shock doubles the productivity of capital goods production only, which of the following correctly describes both the new PPC shape and the new opportunity cost of consumer goods at the former CG-corner production level?

options.label: A
options.text: The new PPC becomes linear because the technology doubles KG productivity uniformly

options.label: B
options.text: The new PPC shifts inward on the CG side because KG is now more attractive to produce

options.label: C
options.text: KG capacity doubles, CG capacity is unchanged, and CG's cost in KG rises

options.label: D
options.text: The new PPC has the same shape with both intercepts doubled

options.label: E
options.text: The opportunity cost of CG is unchanged at the CG-corner because that intercept has not moved

explanation: Technology doubling KG productivity doubles the KG-axis intercept while the CG-axis intercept is unchanged; the PPC pivots outward from the CG-axis intercept. At the CG-corner, the opportunity cost of the last unit of CG in terms of KG increases: previously, producing slightly fewer CG generated KG at the original rate; now, those same resources can produce twice as much KG. The opportunity cost of CG (in terms of KG) has risen.
graphDescription: Original bowed-out PPC with consumer goods (CG) on horizontal axis and capital goods (KG) on vertical axis. Intercepts: CG_max on horizontal, KG_max on vertical. New PPC after technology shock: the KG-axis intercept doubles (to 2×KG_max) while the CG-axis intercept is unchanged. The new PPC is still bowed out but has a higher KG intercept and the same CG intercept — it pivots outward from the CG-axis intercept.

prompt: A policy analyst says: "An economy operating on its PPC is always better off than one operating inside it." A counterargument notes that in some cases, operating inside the PPC may reflect rational choices. Which of the following provides the strongest counterargument to the analyst's claim?

options.label: A
options.text: Operating inside the PPC is always rational because it conserves resources for the future

options.label: B
options.text: Additional measured output may cost more in leisure or environmental quality than it benefits society

options.label: C
options.text: The analyst is completely correct; on-frontier operation is always superior

options.label: D
options.text: The analyst is incorrect; the PPC represents the minimum, not the maximum, level of output

options.label: E
options.text: Operating inside the PPC is better because it reduces inequality

explanation: The PPC measures feasible output, not every dimension of welfare. Extra measured production may require sacrificing leisure or environmental quality that society values more. Thus output alone cannot establish which outcome is better. In the AP model, full-employment output lies on the PPC; the natural rate of unemployment does not imply an interior point.

prompt:
Country Alpha has the following PPC data:

  Option  |  Missiles  |  Bread (millions of loaves)

  D       |  120       |  80

A neighbor offers to trade 1 missile for 1.5 million loaves of bread. Is this a beneficial terms of trade for Alpha to export missiles?

Using the domestic opportunity cost of missiles, evaluate whether Alpha should accept this trade.

options.label: A
options.text: Alpha should accept only if the terms of trade equal the average opportunity cost across all segments

options.label: B
options.text: Trade benefits Alpha only where marginal cost is below 1.5 million loaves per missile

options.label: C

It equals OC in C→D and is less than OC in D→E; alpha benefits from exporting missiles when starting from low missile production levels, but not when already producing many missiles.

prompt: Which of the following most precisely distinguishes between the immediate and long-run effects of a country choosing to produce at a point heavily weighted toward capital goods on its PPC, compared to a point heavily weighted toward consumer goods?

options.label: A
options.text: More current consumption; identical future productive capacity

options.label: B
options.text: Identical current consumption; identical future productive capacity

options.label: C
options.text: Identical current consumption; greater future productive capacity

options.label: D

options.text: Less current consumption; smaller future productive capacity

explanation: This is the fundamental intertemporal trade-off in PPC analysis; choosing the capital-goods-heavy point (K) means producing fewer consumer goods now - the immediate opportunity cost. However, the greater capital accumulation expands future productive capacity, shifting the PPC outward faster in the long run; this enables greater production of both goods in the future; the consumer-goods-heavy point (C) provides more immediate consumption but slower long-run growth.
graphDescription: Two adjacent PPCs — PPC₁ (original) and PPC₂ (future, outward-shifted) — both bowed out. On PPC₁, two points are marked: Point K (near the capital goods corner — high KG, low CG) and Point C (near the consumer goods corner — low KG, high CG). PPC₂ is larger and lies entirely outside PPC₁. An arrow from PPC₁ to PPC₂ represents the outward shift over time. Point K leads to a larger PPC₂ than Point C does, since greater capital accumulation drives faster growth.
